notes.story: [Let the headline sit for a few seconds.] “What do you think they were hiring for?” [Take a guess from the room.] The U.S. Nautical Almanac Office had two vacancies for people to do calculations. The civil service exam included trigonometry and astronomy. Their calculations helped produce tables that sailors used to navigate by the sky.
notes.transition: Let’s look at what a room full of computers looked like.
notes.materials: New York Times, May 2, 1892, p. 8. Scan reproduced by Dan Nguyen: https://danwin.com/2013/02/the-first-mention-of-computer-in-the-new-york-times/ · Page attribution: https://srtate.github.io/old/100.f17/lectures/UNCG-CSC100-F17-LECT3-ComputerScience.pdf

notes.story: [Give the audience several seconds to look.] These are human computers at a NACA flight-test station in 1949. Staff copied readings from film and strips of recording paper. They used slide rules and electric calculators, like the covered Friden at the front, to turn those readings into figures in units the engineers could use. Each test meant more readings and more calculations.
notes.transition: Now look at how that work changed when machines could do more of the arithmetic.

title: From the computer room to your desk

notes.point: From the computer room to your desk
notes.story: [Walk left to right.] These are snapshots of overlapping eras. At NACA, people worked through flight-test calculations with equipment at their desks. Businesses used the IBM 1401 for recurring jobs such as payroll and billing. Imagine collecting a stack of records, running them together and getting a printed result. VisiCalc on the Apple II let the person working on a budget change one assumption and see affected totals update right there. That made it practical to try another number while the question was still fresh. [Optional aside: The U.S. Census Bureau received UNIVAC I in 1951.]
notes.transition: Say you run a small design studio and you’re turning down client work. Could you afford to bring someone on?
notes.materials: NASA: https://www.flickr.com/photos/nasacommons/7538108706 · IBM: https://www.ibm.com/history/1401 · System photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BRL61-IBM_1401.jpg · VisiCalc: https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/1979/ · Later screenshot: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Visicalc.png · UNIVAC: https://www.census.gov/about/history/bureau-history/census-innovations/technology/univac-i.html

notes.story: A small design studio is turning down client work. The owner wants to know how many billable days would cover a hire costing €5,000 per month. Assume four weeks and €500 per billable day. At two days a week, they’re €1,000 short. Ask “What if they can bill three days a week?” [Advance.] Revenue rises to €6,000 and they’re €1,000 above cost. Ask “What if it takes a few months to get that busy?” [Pause.] The spreadsheet lets the owner explore what would have to be true for the hire to pay for itself.
notes.transition: Look at the questions the studio can now try.

notes.story: Start with the question in the overlap. The owner can check whether the hire covers its cost. [Advance.] Watch the circle grow around the other two questions. What if work starts slowly? What if we hire part-time? With a spreadsheet, running another scenario is easy enough to try.
notes.transition: [Advance and keep the expanded diagram in view.]

notes.story: The spreadsheet made it easy enough to try another assumption. AI can make it easy enough to try a first version of a tool. In both cases, lowering the cost of the experiment changes which ideas we get to test. [Advance.] The same studio wants to spend less time writing quotes. A reusable template is already practical to try. What about a small tool that takes a client brief and starts a quote and project checklist? [Advance.] Put a draft quote in front of someone who writes quotes and see whether it saves them work.
notes.transition: One of those ideas started with something I wanted to do at the gym.

title: GymNative · A workout logger that knows your gym

notes.point: GymNative · A workout logger that knows your gym
notes.story: “I wanted to put the paper aside, log what I lifted on my phone, and see whether I was getting stronger.” On the left, I’m entering 35 kilos and 12 reps on the leg press. On the right, I can look back and see the weight I logged over three sample workouts. [Advance.] This is the Haguegym view. The branding, the machine circuit and its starting exercise are already there. The gym sets up the equipment and workout once. Members can open it and get straight to logging.
notes.transition: A general tracker could already do part of this. What would make a logger for one gym worth trying?
notes.materials: Local Haguegym captures with fictional workouts.

title: A logger set up for this gym

notes.point: A logger set up for this gym
notes.story: Using a general tracker is already practical. [Advance.] AI-assisted development made a first version tailored to one gym practical to try. The pilot question is “Will members come back and log their next workout?” The work is deciding what the gym should configure, how a member opens it and logs a first set, and what we would need to see to keep going. I’d look for members returning to log another workout, and ask where anyone got stuck. [Confirm the Haguegym pilot status before presenting. Keep outcomes open.]
notes.transition: At Zoundio, the question was how the existing team could reach people who wanted to play on a computer.

title: Zoundio · Guitar gameplay in the browser

notes.point: Zoundio · Guitar gameplay in the browser
notes.story: People had long asked to play on a computer. We already had guitar gameplay on iOS and Android, and each app needs ongoing support. A dedicated PC app would have added a platform with its own expertise and upkeep. [Advance.] Here’s the upcoming version running in a browser, on the Add Index Finger lesson. AI-assisted development helped make it practical for the existing team to pursue web gameplay. [Confirm release wording and timing before presenting.]
notes.transition: Here, the additional thing worth trying was a way to play on a computer.
notes.materials: Public Gibson App mobile gameplay crop with App Store and Google Play badges, followed by the presenter-supplied Add Index Finger browser gameplay capture. The images show different lessons. Confirm release wording and timing.

notes.story: Supporting iOS and Android is already part of the work. [Advance.] The existing team can now pursue another way for people to play, by bringing gameplay to the browser. That opens a way to reach people who want to play on a computer.
notes.transition: We’ve seen what this opens up for a gym and for a team making music software. Now let’s look at something everyone here already uses.
